title: Donor Safety at the Chair: Blood Volume, Circuit Limits, Reactions and Draw Time
summary: Estimate donor blood volume with Gilcher’s rule of fives, apply the extracorporeal volume limit, tell hypovolemic from vasovagal reactions and manage them, and see why draw-time limits depend on the component being made.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 42 Hit 3 (Gilcher’s rule of fives), Hit 10 (extracorporeal circuit limit), Hit 18 (whole-blood collection time), Hit 19 (vasovagal reaction) and Trap 4 (hypovolemic vs vasovagal), checked against Potente 2020, Basu 2014, Philip 2013, Philip 2014, Basavarajegowda 2024 and Rajkumar 2024. Qualifications: the reviewer’s single rule “collection must complete within 10 minutes; a 16-minute draw is discarded” is replaced by component-specific limits (one published case report summarising earlier literature: over 10/12 min unsuitable for platelets and over 13/15 min unsuitable for FFP, by bag size); UK and Council of Europe limits could not be read (register flag rv-draw-time-component-limits). The reviewer’s “check the pulse” fork is taught as a clue, not proof, because presyncope signs include sympathetic features (tachycardia if standing), the slow heart rate plays only a minor role in the faint, and in an apheresis series both reactions are first managed the same way (rv-vasovagal-pulse-clue). The 10.5 mL/kg figure is taught as 15% of 70 mL/kg; its attribution to AABB standards was not verified (AABB Standards not openly available). The reviewer’s “supine with legs elevated” is taught as the head-down (Trendelenburg) position described in the source read. Not taught: ACE-inhibitor withholding (Hit 6), directed donors (Hit 21), the Number Vault table. US/AABB and Indian-standard figures only; Philippine rules were not checked.

objectives: Estimate a donor’s total blood volume with Gilcher’s rule of fives and apply a 15% extracorporeal volume limit.
Distinguish hypovolemic from vasovagal donor reactions by autonomic signature, and describe first-line management.
Explain why whole-blood draw-time limits are component-specific rather than a single discard rule.

scenes.title: Three donors, one shift
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three donors on one shift — (1) a thin 50-kg woman booked for plateletpheresis on an intermittent-flow separator whose circuit holds about 360 mL; (2) a whole-blood donor in a 450 mL bag whose sluggish draw finishes at 14 minutes; (3) a donor who, midway through a whole-blood draw, turns pale and sweaty, feels sick, and has a pulse of 48. Question token: “Safe circuit? Usable unit? Which reaction?”

cues.text: Three donors, one shift. A thin fifty-kilogram woman is booked for plateletpheresis on a machine whose circuit holds about three hundred and sixty millilitres.
A whole-blood draw into a four-hundred-and-fifty-millilitre bag runs slowly and finishes at fourteen minutes. A third donor turns pale and sweaty, with a pulse of forty-eight.
Is the circuit safe for her, what can the slow unit still be used for, and which reaction is this?

props.label: Safe circuit? Usable unit? Which reaction?

scenes.title: How big is the tank?
scenes.altText: Schematic: a body outline beside a table, Gilcher’s rule of fives (estimated total blood volume in mL per kg of body weight): males — obese 60, thin 65, normal 70, muscular 75; females — 5 less in each category (55, 60, 65, 70). A note: other estimates exist, such as height-and-weight formulas used in donor studies, and simple per-kilogram rules can overestimate blood volume in obese people. A second card: apheresis aims to keep the extracorporeal volume, the blood outside the body in the circuit at any moment, at no more than about 15% of total blood volume. Worked example: 15% of 70 mL/kg is 10.5 mL/kg.

cues.text: Every donor safety limit starts with blood volume. Gilcher’s rule of fives estimates it in millilitres per kilogram: for men, obese sixty, thin sixty-five, normal seventy, muscular seventy-five.
For women, subtract five from each: obese fifty-five, thin sixty, normal sixty-five, muscular seventy. Multiply by body weight to estimate the total.
It is only an estimate. Donor studies also use formulas based on height and weight. One forensic study warns that simple per-kilogram rules tend to overestimate blood volume in obese people.

During apheresis, the aim is to keep the blood outside the body, the extracorporeal volume, at or below about fifteen percent of total blood volume. For a donor at seventy millilitres per kilogram, that works out to ten point five millilitres per kilogram.

props.label: An estimate: other formulas use height and weight

scenes.title: When the donor reacts
scenes.altText: Two-column schematic of autonomic signatures. Left, hypovolemic: falling blood pressure unloads the baroreceptors; sympathetic output rises — faster heart rate, vasoconstriction. Right, vasovagal: parasympathetic (vagal) output rises and sympathetic tone is withdrawn — slow heart rate, vasodilation, hypotension; presyncope signs are light-headedness, nausea, sweating and pallor. Timeline strip: reactions rise toward the end of the draw, peak around needle removal, and many occur after the needle is out, in the chair or the refreshment area, with some delayed hours later off-site. Risk card: low estimated blood volume, low weight, first-time and female donors had higher reaction rates in one study; in apheresis, one research group proposed that a larger share of blood in the circuit explains more hypotensive reactions in women and older donors.

cues.text: Two reactions can look alike. In a hypovolemic reaction, falling pressure unloads the baroreceptors, and sympathetic output rises: the heart speeds up and vessels constrict.
In a vasovagal reaction, vagal output rises and sympathetic tone is withdrawn: the heart slows and vessels relax. Warning signs are light-headedness, nausea, sweating and pallor.
Timing matters. Reactions rise toward the end of the draw, peak around needle removal, and many happen after the needle is out, some hours later and away from the site.

Risk rises with low blood volume. In one large study, donors with a low estimated blood volume, low weight, first-time donors and women reacted more often. In apheresis, one group proposed that a bigger share of blood in the circuit causes more hypotension.

props.label: Peak near needle removal · many after the needle is out

props.title: Higher risk
lines: Low blood volume · low weight · first-time · female

scenes.title: Managing the chair and the clock
scenes.altText: Left card, managing a reaction (described in an apheresis series): pause the procedure and start a fluid infusion; if the cause is hypovolemia, blood pressure should rise and pulse fall; if it is vasovagal, they may not. For vasovagal: head-down (Trendelenburg) position, cold compresses to forehead and neck, and reassurance. Right card, draw time (one published case report summarising earlier literature): average draw 5–10 minutes; beyond 10 min (350 mL bag) or 12 min (450 mL bag) not suitable for platelet concentrates; beyond 13 or 15 min not suitable for fresh frozen plasma; a slow 12-minute draw in one case report produced a large clot in the bag. Bottom: hook answers — (1) 50 kg × 60 mL/kg = 3,000 mL; 15% = 450 mL, so a 360 mL circuit is within limit; (2) 14 min in a 450 mL bag: no platelet concentrate, still inside the FFP limit; (3) vasovagal.

cues.text: In one apheresis series, both reactions are first managed the same way: pause the procedure and start a fluid infusion. If the cause is volume loss, the pressure should rise and the pulse fall. A vasovagal reaction may not respond.
For a vasovagal reaction, lay the donor head-down, apply cold compresses to the forehead and neck, and reassure them.

The clock matters too. A whole-blood draw usually takes five to ten minutes. In one published summary, units from draws over ten or twelve minutes, by bag size, were unsuitable for platelets, and over thirteen or fifteen minutes, unsuitable for fresh frozen plasma.

Hook answers. Fifty kilograms times sixty is three thousand millilitres, and fifteen percent is four hundred and fifty, so the circuit is within limit. Under that summary, the fourteen-minute unit cannot make platelets. And the donor with a pulse of forty-eight is vasovagal.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Hypovolemic and vasovagal reactions are the same” (✓ opposite autonomic signatures — sympathetic tachycardia vs vagal bradycardia — but presyncope signs reflect both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation and the slow heart rate plays only a minor part in the faint, so the pulse is a clue, not proof); “Any draw over 10 minutes is discarded” (✓ in the summary read, limits are component-specific and depend on bag size; standards differ); “Reactions only happen while the needle is in” (✓ many happen after needle removal, some hours later and off-site).

cues.text: Trap one: hypovolemic and vasovagal reactions are the same. No: volume loss drives the heart faster, vagal reactions slow it. But warning signs are mixed, and the slow pulse is often a minor part of a faint, so the pulse is a clue, not proof.
Trap two: any draw over ten minutes is discarded. No: in the summary read, the limits depend on the component being made and the bag size, and standards differ.
Trap three: reactions only happen while the needle is in. No: many occur after the needle is out, some hours later and away from the donor site.

props.title: ✗ “Hypovolemic = vasovagal.”
lines: ✓ Fast pulse vs slow pulse; a clue, not proof

scenes.title: Fives, fifteen, fork
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “FIVES size the tank (Gilcher: 70 for a normal man, minus 5 for a woman, plus or minus 5 for build); FIFTEEN percent may sit in the circuit; at the FORK, read the pulse — racing means volume, crashing means vagus.” Tokens: fives = blood volume · fifteen = circuit · fork = pulse. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: fives size the tank, seventy for a normal man, minus five for a woman, and five up or down for build. Fifteen percent may sit in the circuit. At the fork, read the pulse: racing means volume, crashing means vagus.

Where it breaks: blood volume rules are estimates; a standing donor with vasovagal signs can have a fast pulse, and the slow pulse is a minor part of a faint, so the fork is a clue; and draw-time limits differ by component and by standard.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Pulse is a clue: standing donors can be fast
Draw-time limits vary by component and standard

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Gilcher fives size the tank · circuit ≤ ~15% of total blood volume”, “Fast pulse = volume, slow pulse = vagal · draw-time limits are component-specific”.

cues.text: Estimate blood volume with Gilcher’s rule of fives, keep the apheresis circuit to about fifteen percent of it, read a fainting donor’s pulse as a clue to volume loss or a vagal reaction, and remember that published draw-time limits differ by component rather than setting one discard time.

props.label: Gilcher fives size the tank · circuit ≤ ~15% of blood volume
Fast pulse = volume · slow pulse = vagal · draw limits by component

explanation.what: Plain language: before blood leaves a donor, you need to know roughly how much they have, how much can safely be outside the body in a machine at once, how to recognise and treat a faint, and how long a draw can take before some products can no longer be made from it. Scientific terms: total blood volume (TBV), Gilcher’s rule of fives, extracorporeal volume (ECV), hypovolemic reaction, vasovagal reaction (VVR), baroreceptor reflex, presyncope, Trendelenburg position, draw (bleed) time, platelet concentrate, fresh frozen plasma (FFP).
explanation.why: Small donors have a small total blood volume, so a fixed circuit or collection volume is a bigger share of what they have, and reactions are more common. Vasovagal reactions are a reflex: rising vagal output slows the heart and withdrawn sympathetic tone relaxes vessels, while volume loss triggers the opposite, sympathetic, compensation. Slow flow can mean poorer mixing with anticoagulant and activation of clotting in the bag; in the summary read, the time limit is shortest for platelet concentrates and longer for fresh frozen plasma.
explanation.measure: Gilcher (mL/kg): men obese 60, thin 65, normal 70, muscular 75; women 5 less in each. ECV kept at or below about 15% of TBV (15% × 70 mL/kg = 10.5 mL/kg). One published summary: average draw 5–10 min; over 10 min (350 mL bag) or 12 min (450 mL bag) unsuitable for platelet concentrates; over 13 or 15 min unsuitable for FFP. Reaction management (apheresis series): pause, start a fluid infusion; vasovagal additionally head-down position, cold compresses, reassurance.
explanation.differs: Hypovolemic (sympathetic: faster pulse, vasoconstriction; pressure rises and pulse falls with fluid) vs vasovagal (parasympathetic: slower pulse, vasodilation; may not respond to fluid). Gilcher’s body-build factors vs height-and-weight formulas. Platelet vs FFP draw-time limits.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: calculate TBV or the maximum ECV for a given donor; name the reaction from pallor, sweating and a slow pulse and pick the management; decide what a slow-draw unit can still be used for.

questions.stem: A thin 50-kg woman is evaluated for plateletpheresis. Using Gilcher’s rule of fives and an extracorporeal volume limit of 15% of total blood volume, what is the most blood that should be outside her body at one time?

options.rationale: Correct. Thin woman = 60 mL/kg; 50 × 60 = 3,000 mL; 15% of 3,000 = 450 mL.
Incorrect. This uses 10.5 mL/kg, which assumes 70 mL/kg (a normal-build man) and overestimates a thin woman’s blood volume.
Incorrect. This is her estimated total blood volume, not the circuit limit.
Incorrect. This uses 65 mL/kg (a normal-build woman): 3,250 × 15% is about 488 mL, not the thin-build factor of 60 mL/kg.

questions.stem: Midway through a whole-blood donation, a donor becomes pale and sweaty, feels nauseated, and her pulse falls to 48 with low blood pressure. What is the most likely reaction and appropriate first management?

options.text: Vasovagal reaction: pause the draw, head-down position, cold compresses to forehead and neck, reassurance
options.rationale: Correct. A slow pulse with hypotension, pallor, sweating and nausea fits rising vagal output; these are the measures described in the source read.

options.text: Hypovolemic reaction: expect a racing pulse, so continue the draw
options.rationale: Incorrect. Volume loss drives sympathetic compensation and a faster pulse; this donor’s pulse is slow, and a reacting donor’s procedure should be paused.
Incorrect. Citrate reactions come from the citrate anticoagulant returned to donors during apheresis, not from a whole-blood draw, and cause symptoms such as perioral paresthesias.

options.text: Normal response: no action until she loses consciousness
options.rationale: Incorrect. Presyncope signs come 30–60 seconds before a faint, so measures should start now rather than after she loses consciousness.

questions.stem: Under the draw-time limits summarised by Rajkumar and colleagues (2024), a 450 mL whole-blood unit took 14 minutes to collect. What is the best disposition?

options.text: Do not prepare a platelet concentrate; the draw is still within the FFP limit
options.rationale: Correct. For a 450 mL bag, over 12 minutes rules out platelet concentrates, and the FFP limit is 15 minutes.

options.text: Discard the whole unit because it exceeded 10 minutes
options.rationale: Incorrect. The limits cited are component-specific and depend on bag size; there is no single 10-minute discard rule in that summary.
Incorrect. 14 minutes exceeds the 12-minute platelet limit for a 450 mL bag.
Incorrect. This reverses the limits: platelets have the shorter limit.

references.citation: Potente S, Ramsthaler F, Kettner M, Sauer P, Schmidt P. Relative blood loss in forensic medicine-do we need a change in doctrine? Int J Legal Med. 2020;134(3):1123-1131. doi:10.1007/s00414-020-02260-w
references.usedFor: Gilcher’s rule of five (table of blood volume formulas, citing Gilcher 1996): normal ♂ 70 / ♀ 65, thin 65 / 60, obese 60 / 55, muscular 75 / 70 mL/kg; other TBV formulas exist; for overweight and obese people, overestimation of TBV is likely unless BMI-adapted algorithms are used.

references.citation: Basu D, Kulkarni R. Overview of blood components and their preparation. Indian J Anaesth. 2014;58(5):529-537. doi:10.4103/0019-5049.144647
references.usedFor: Apheresis goal not to exceed an ECV of 15% of total blood volume (wording in the source is partly ambiguous); citrate toxicity in apheresis donors manifests as perioral paresthesia and tingling.

references.citation: Philip J, Sarkar RS, Pathak A. Adverse events associated with apheresis procedures: Incidence and relative frequency. Asian J Transfus Sci. 2013;7(1):37-41. doi:10.4103/0973-6247.106730
references.usedFor: Hypovolemia → sympathetic compensation; citrate from the apheresis return causes symptoms including perioral paresthesias; vasovagal → increased parasympathetic output, slower heart rate, decreased vascular tone; both treated by pausing and giving fluid (BP rises, pulse falls if hypovolemic; may not if vasovagal); vasovagal: Trendelenburg, cold compresses to forehead and neck, reassurance; lower circulating volume → larger share of blood extracorporeal → more hypotension (hypothesis of Tomita et al., as reported); separator ECVs (MCS+ ~360 mL; CS3000 200–250 mL).

references.citation: Philip J, Sarkar RS, Jain N. A single-centre study of vasovagal reaction in blood donors: Influence of age, sex, donation status, weight, total blood volume and volume of blood collected. Asian J Transfus Sci. 2014;8(1):43-46. doi:10.4103/0973-6247.126690
references.usedFor: VVR rate 1.23% of 88,201 donations; low estimated blood volume (< 4.5 L), weight < 55 kg, first-time and female donors had higher VVR rates; EBV calculated by a height-and-weight formula; VVR caused by parasympathetic stimulation augmented by relative hypovolemia; the vascular response (vasodilation, pooling, hypotension) is the main cause of the faint, and the parasympathetic slowing of heart rate plays only a minor role.

references.citation: Basavarajegowda A, Nalini YC. Syncopal reactions in blood donors: Pathophysiology, clinical course, and features. Asian J Transfus Sci. 2024;18(2):296-302. doi:10.4103/ajts.ajts_167_21
references.usedFor: Complete donation typically takes 7–10 min; presyncope begins 30–60 s before syncope; reactions rise toward the end of donation and peak around needle removal; many occur after the needle is out and some 4–6 h later off-site, with higher injury rates; baroreceptor unloading → sympathetic vasoconstriction and tachycardia; vasovagal → vagal bradycardia and withdrawn sympathetic tone; presyncope signs (light-headedness, nausea, sweating, pallor) reflect both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation, and sinus tachycardia is noted if the donor is standing; syncope relieved by moving from upright to supine.

references.citation: Rajkumar A, Vetriveeran S, Iyyapan SK, Haran Annadurai H, James S. Clot in the Blood Bag: A Case Report. Cureus. 2024;16(9):e69452. doi:10.7759/cureus.69452
references.usedFor: Average draw time 5–10 min; draws beyond 10 and 12 min (350 and 450 mL bags) not suitable for platelet concentrates, beyond 13 and 15 min not suitable for FFP (citing a 2021 Transfus Clin Biol article, not read; not a standard text); case of a 12-minute slow draw (350 mL) producing a 6 × 7 cm clot.

claims.text: Gilcher’s rule of fives values for men and women by body build.
ECV kept at or below about 15% of total blood volume; 15% × 70 mL/kg = 10.5 mL/kg; one group proposed that smaller-volume donors have a larger share in the circuit and more hypotensive reactions.
The 10.5 mL/kg figure is the AABB donor extracorporeal limit.
claims.note: AABB Standards are not openly available; not taught as an AABB rule, only as arithmetic.

claims.text: Hypovolemic reaction is sympathetic (faster pulse, vasoconstriction); vasovagal is parasympathetic (slower pulse, decreased tone); presyncope signs are mixed, a standing donor can be tachycardic, and the cardiac slowing plays a minor role in the faint.
Reaction timing (peak around needle removal, many afterwards, some delayed off-site) and risk factors (low EBV, low weight, first-time, female).
Pause and give fluid; response differs by cause; vasovagal: head-down position, cold compresses, reassurance.
claims.note: Source describes apheresis donors; applied to whole-blood donors as the general approach.

claims.text: Usual draw 5–10 min; component-specific draw-time limits for platelets and FFP by bag size; slow draws can clot.
Citrate reactions in apheresis donors cause symptoms such as perioral paresthesias (question rationale).

accuracyFlags.issue: Reviewer gives one rule (collection must finish within 10 minutes; a 16-minute draw is discarded). The source read (a case report citing earlier literature, not a standard) describes component-specific limits by bag size (platelets 10/12 min, FFP 13/15 min); UK and Council of Europe limits could not be read. The lesson teaches component-specific limits.

Reviewer’s “racing points to volume loss, crashing points to vagal” is taught as a clue: presyncope signs reflect both sympathetic and parasympathetic activation (sinus tachycardia if standing), and the vascular response, not the slow heart rate, is the main cause of the faint (Philip 2014); and in an apheresis series both reactions are first managed by pausing and starting a fluid infusion.

The 10.5 mL/kg AABB attribution could not be verified from an open source; the lesson teaches the 15% of total blood volume goal and derives 10.5 mL/kg as 15% of 70 mL/kg. This is a US/AABB figure; Philippine rules are not covered.
